author: Olivieri & Filigenzi
name_in_asr: Butkara I; Tolo (Songyun); Dhumat'ala (O rgyan pa)
asr_identification: Butkara I, Mingora, Swat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, identified with Songyun's Tolo monastery
evidence: Butkara I, excavated by Faccenna 1956–62: an unbroken sequence from the 3rd c. BC to the 10th/11th c. AD in five building periods of the Great Stūpa; the period of Great Stūpa 4 runs from the end of the 2nd/early 3rd c. to the 7th c. AD, with a shift to stucco and kanjur, reuse of earlier schist panels in niches with reliquary recesses, and a restoration after collapse probably caused by an earthquake (coin deposit). The equation with Songyun's Tolo and O rgyan pa's Dhumat'ala is after Tucci 1978 and Faccenna 1980–81.
quote: Identified with the Tolo visited by Songyun and the Dhumat’ala of the Tibetan pilgrim O rgyan pa (Tucci 1978: 60-61; Faccenna 1980-81: [4] 756, n. 1.), Butkara I was excavated…The long archaeological sequence, stretching from the third century BC to the tenth/eleventh century AD…(from the end of the second/early third century to the seventh century AD)
note: Not a Xiyu ji identification: Butkara I is equated with Songyun's Tolo, not with Xuanzang's Kṣānti stūpa (03.01.02), for which the study keeps Butkara I only as Tucci's candidate (and only with Mingora as capital). Adds that the Great Stūpa was still maintained and redecorated into the 7th c., so a working monument at Mingora in 630; compatible with the study's Mingora capital (03.01.01a) but no new evidence for either identification. No change.

author: Olivieri & Filigenzi
asr_identification: Barikot, Swat; Gumbat and Amluk-dara 5 km SW and SE of it
evidence: IAMP excavations: the walled city of Barikot was founded c. 6th c. BC, refortified mid-2nd c. BC, its lower town abandoned at the end of the 3rd c. AD after two earthquakes and deserted by the mid-4th c.; only a small fortified cluster at the foot of the acropolis (BKG 2) lasted through a Shahi phase to Ghaznavid times. Over 100 monastic settlements in under 100 km² of its countryside, most founded before the 2nd c. AD; Gumbat and Amluk-dara renovated after the 3rd-c. crisis and abandoned c. 10th c.
quote: The lower quarters of the ancient city were eventually abandoned at the end of the third century after massive…a smaller fortified cluster of buildings was built at the foot of the ancient acropolis (BKG 2) and lasted – through a well-documented Shahi phase – until Ghaznavid times
note: Barikot is not named in the Xiyu ji and no Xuanzang place is located here. Context only: a Swat town deserted long before 630 while its rural Buddhist sanctuaries (Gumbat, Amluk-dara) remained in use to c. 10th c.

author: Behrendt
asr_identification: the cruciform stūpa at Shāh-jī-kī-ḍherī, Peshawar (Kuwayama 1997)
evidence: Behrendt (in the same volume) cites Xuanzang's restoration of Kaniṣka's fire-damaged stūpa (Beal 1884: 103) as late Buddhist activity in Gandhāra and identifies it, after Kuwayama 1997, as probably the cruciform stūpa at Shāh-jī-kī-ḍherī. No new evidence.
quote: and of the restoration of Kaniṣka’s stūpa, which had been damaged by fire (Beal 1884: 103), that is probably the cruciform stūpa at Shāh-jī-kī-ḍherī (Kuwayama 1997)
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Shah-ji-ki-Dheri); a citation of Kuwayama only. No change.

author: Behrendt
evidence: Behrendt takes Po-lu-sha, where Xuanzang found a monastery with fifty monks (Beal 1884: 112), as 'likely Sahrī-Bahlol' after Errington 1993. No argument or evidence given.
quote: He notes other activity in the city of Po-lu-sha, likely Sahrī-Bahlol (Errington 1993), where he encountered a monastery with fifty priests (Beal 1884: 112).
note: Differs from the study (Shahbaz Garhi) by following Errington's Shahr-i Bahlol, the rival the study already records (via Neelis 2011). A second citation, not new evidence; Errington's own reasoning is quoted in rienjang_stewart2019_geography:1–2. No change.

author: Behrendt
asr_identification: Mekhasanda, in the hills above Shābāz Garhī, Peshawar basin
evidence: From Mizuno 1969: foundation in Behrendt's phase II (coins of Kaniṣka I and Huviṣka, early schist sculpture), refurbishment and late phase III additions (stepped small stūpas, image shrines, >180 stucco fragments against c. 22 schist icons, two monumental image shrines with colossal heads); latest coins Vāsudeva imitations (AD 268–308 or later) and one Kushano-Sasanian. Patronage continued 'in the late part of phase III' (3rd–5th c. on his chronology).
quote: the small, relatively simple complex of Mekhasanda in the hills above the town of Shābāz Garhī…demonstrates that Mekhasanda was still receiving patronage in the late part of phase III
note: Site chronology of the study's Daṇḍaloka site (Mekha-Sanda, 02.04.15); Behrendt does not connect it with Xuanzang and the dating neither confirms nor excludes a monastery there in 630. Context only.

author: Khan Khattak
asr_identification: Sahri Bahlol, Mardan district (Errington 1993, quoted); not Palo Dheri
evidence: Khan Khattak rejects Cunningham's and Watters' Palusha = Palo Dheri as resting only on distances, and quotes Errington (1993: 63), who takes Pa-lu-sha as Sahri Bahlol and derives Daṇḍaloka from it. The quoted passage states Sahri Bahlol as a premise ('if the latter is identified as Sahri Bahlol'); Errington's argument for it is not given.
quote: Furthermore, the identification of Palusha with Palo Dheri by Cunningham and Watters (Watters 1904: 217) merely on the basis of a correspondence in distances is also unreliable…for if the latter is identified as Sahri Bahlol, it seems that the former must be equated with the Takht-i-Bāhi hill
note: Differs from the study (Shahbaz Garhi): reports Errington's Shahr-i Bahlol, the rival the study records as 'unread'; now her words are available in quotation (1993: 63), but only as a premise for Daṇḍaloka. The rejection of Palo Dheri agrees with the study (Cunningham himself abandoned it). Alternative stays recorded; no change of rating.

author: Khan Khattak
asr_identification: Takht-i-Bāhī hill, Mardan district (Errington 1993, quoted); the cave c. 2 km W of the Takht-i-Bāhī sacred area (Khan Khattak)
evidence: Errington (1993: 63, quoted): if Pa-lu-sha is Sahri Bahlol, Daṇḍaloka 'above 20 li' NE must be the Takht-i-Bāhī hill; discrepancy in distance and direction explained by a walk of 2½ miles to the foot of the ridge and then E to the site on its N slope; a corroded copper coin of Agathocles (c. 190–180 BC) from the subterranean vaulted chambers on the E side suggests an early foundation, so the stūpa could be 'Aśokan' as Xuanzang says; the subterranean cells perhaps the Viśvantara cave. Khan Khattak finds this 'logical' though 'far from certain', but places the cave instead at a rock cave c. 2 km W of the sacred area across two peaks, with remains below it and Buddhist structures on the ridge (fig. 7).
quote: a note should perhaps be added regarding the Tan-to-lo-ka mountain visited by Xuanzang…for a corroded copper coin of this ruler was excavated from the subterranean vaulted chambers on the east side of the site…If we have to look for this so-called cave, it can be seen not very far away from the sacred area of the Takht-i-Bāhī Buddhist complex, to the west across two peaks
note: Differs from the study (Mekha-Sanda, NE of Shahbaz Garhi): Takht-i-Bāhī follows only from Errington's Sahri Bahlol for 02.04.14, and the Takht-i-Bāhī monastery lies c. 4–5 km NW of Sahri Bahlol, not NE (the 'discrepancy' Errington concedes). An Agathocles coin dates the site's beginnings, not its name. A dependent alternative to record beside Mekha-Sanda; place stays as rated (probable for Mekha-Sanda only if Shahbaz Garhi holds).

author: Baums
asr_identification: Oḍi = Uḍḍiyāna, i.e. Swat; Tira a city of the Oḍi kings (inscriptions from Swat)
evidence: Three Gāndhārī inscriptions name the Oḍi royal house (1st c. AD), 'almost certainly' Sanskrit Uḍḍiyāna = Swat; Tira, named in two inscriptions from Swat connected with the Oḍi kings (CKI 334, 401), appears to have been their capital or a major city.
quote: The second name is consistently spelled Oḍi (in three inscriptions),5 and can almost certainly be connected with Sanskrit Uḍḍiyāna, i.e. Swat…Tira, attested in two inscriptions from Swat connected to the Oḍi royal house (CKI 334 and 401), appears to have been the capital or at least a major city of this dynasty.
note: Agrees (Udyāna = Swat): an early epigraphic form of the country's name from Swat itself. Tira is a 1st-c. Oḍi city, unlocated here; no bearing on Xuanzang's capital 瞢揭釐 (03.01.01a). No change.

author: Baums
evidence: The city's name in Gāndhārī inscriptions: Takṣaśila (CKI 60, 66, 233), Takhaśila (CKI 46, 65, 99), adjective Takṣaïlaa (CKI 68); a reliquary found at Taxila (CKI 60) names a donor resident of another city, Ṇoacaa; Chaḍaśila (CKI 172) and Cukhsa (CKI 46, 63) were places near Taxila. Findspots of the other inscriptions are not given here.
quote: Another major city just to the east of Gandhāra proper was Taxila, the name of which is amply attested in inscriptions as Takṣaśila (CKI 60, 66, 233), Takhaśila (46, 65, 99), and as the adjective Takṣaïlaa (CKI 68)
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Taxila ruins); the name in local Kharoṣṭhī inscriptions underlies the identification. No new site evidence in this item; no change.

author: Baums
asr_identification: Kaniṣkapura a city at Peshawar (CKI 145); Avaśaüra a city at Charsadda (CKI 178); Pokhaladi = Puṣkalāvatī in Gāndhārī avadānas
evidence: Cities called nagara/pura in the Gāndhārī inscriptions include Avaśaüra at Charsadda (CKI 178) and Kaniṣkapura at Peshawar (CKI 145); the British Library Gāndhārī avadānas (CKM 2, 14) name Pokhaladi = Puṣkalāvatī, without location.
quote: Other settlements called ‘city’ (nagara or pura) in the epigraphic corpus include Ari-ṇayara in Swat (CKI 828), Avaśaüra at Charsadda (CKI 178) and Kaniṣkapura at Peshawar (CKI 145)…mentions of Pokhaladi (Sanskrit Puṣkalāvatī) in CKM 2 and 14
note: Neither identification changes: the Kushan-period city names at Peshawar (Kaniṣkapura) and Charsadda (Avaśaüra) are not the names Xuanzang uses (布路沙布邏, 布色羯邏伐底), and Pokhaladi is attested only in narrative texts. (CKI 145 is, in Baums & Glass's catalogue, the Kaniṣka reliquary from Shāh-jī-kī-ḍherī, which also names Kaniṣka's vihāra, 02.04.06; that is outside this item, verify before use.) Agrees with Peshawar and Charsadda as rated.

author: Yatoo
asr_identification: Kashmir entered by the Jhelum valley route at Baramulla; Hushkapura = Ushkar, Baramulla town (after Stein)
evidence: After Stein's Rājataraṅgiṇī (2005 reprint: 14–15, 83): Xuanzang came from Urasa (Hazara), entered Kashmir at Baramulla and spent the night at Hushkapura, modern Ushkar; Ou-k'ong took the same route in 759. Ushkar is an excavated Buddhist site in Baramulla town (Garrick 1882; later Sahni) with rubble structures and plain terracotta floor tiles comparable with Harwan and Kanispora, dated 1st–5th c. AD. (Yatoo dates Xuanzang to the '6th century'.)
quote: Pilgrims like Hiuen Tsiang (a Buddhist pilgrim from China) travelled through this route in 6th century AD from Urasa (modern Hazara) and entered Kashmir through Baramulla spending the night at Hushkapura (modern Ushkar) in Baramulla District (Stein 2005: 14-15, 83)…Mr. Garrick undertook excavations at Ushkar in Baramulla town to expose the structural ruins of Buddhist period.
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Kashmir, entered by the W gate at Baramula). Adds the Life's 護瑟迦羅寺 = Huṣkapura = Ushkar (Stein) with an excavated Buddhist site there (Kushan-period structures and tiles), which the 03.06 note does not mention; no inscription names it and the dating stops at the 5th c. on Yatoo's summary. No change of rating.

author: Yatoo
asr_identification: N (right) bank of the Jhelum c. 3–6 km below Baramulla: sites 10.1–10.5 (Pari, Noogul, Fathgarh temple, Shalwajin, Malsum)
evidence: Systematic transect survey 2009: transect 10 (9 km from near Heevan to the Jhelum bank opposite Khadanyar) found five sites, all pottery scatters except the excavated Fathgarh temple (pre-Kārkoṭa, c. 550 AD): Shalwajin in Sheeri village (34°11.029′N 74°18.596′E), 300 m NE of the Jhelum, early-historic and later-historic pottery (parallels Harwan 100–500 AD, Fathgarh 550 AD); Malsum, Pari, Noogul later-historic (6th–10th c.). No Buddhist structures recorded; two rubble structural bases elsewhere in the district (sites 4.3, 9.2) are of undetermined function.
quote: This site was located in the middle of Sheeri village 3 kms south east of Heevan village. Jhelum River flows 300 meters towards SW of this site…The pottery collected showed resemblance with Harwan (100 AD to 500 AD) and Fathgarh (550 AD) pottery…This is a reported and excavated site in the village of Fathgarh boasting a large temple dating to 550 AD of pre-Karkota period.
note: Site-level background for the Baramula–Rampur stretch (study and Mizutani): the survey's N-bank sites just below Baramula show early-historic to 6th–10th-c. occupation but no monastery; it did not reach Zehanpore (c. 5 km further W). No candidate; the study's assessment (unlocated, Zehanpore on position only, low) stands.
